subject: Thermal carve-out & throughput sizing for private GPU pool — Orchid AI
messages:
From: Evan Turner <evan.turner@orchid-ai.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-12-09T14:12:00Z
Subject: Private GPU pool: thermal behavior and throughput targets

Hi Stephanie —

Thanks again for the intro call this morning. As discussed, we're preparing an on-prem VPC deployment with Redwood Dedicated for a regulated EU customer and want a concise capacity plan that specifically accounts for:

- Sustained throughput targets: Orchids' production workload mixes to match 1,200 concurrent user sessions (median seq ~512, 95th seq ~2048).
- Thermal/derate behavior: racks will be in a constrained datacenter (30C ambient) and vendor spec indicates GPU thermal plateaus after ~90 minutes of sustained full-GPU work.
- Network egress pressure: each rack has a 40 Gbps uplink; we'd like recommendations for safe NIC headroom.
- Workload carve-outs: how to prioritize low-latency chat vs batch embedding and background rerank without over-provisioning.

Attached is a 24h telemetry snapshot from our staging cluster (orchid-telemetry-snapshot-20261208.csv). Can your team return a short runbook / sizing artifact we can include in the security review? We're targetting an initial committed pool for Q1.

Thanks,
Evan Turner
Head of Platform
Orchid AI

Subject: Re: Private GPU pool: thermal behavior and throughput targets

Hi Evan —

Appreciate the telemetry. I pulled the CSV and skimmed the 95th-sched-length and long-tail utilization. Early takeaways: the mix is clearly tri-modal (interactive chat, mid-size rerank, large embed batches) which is good for carving.

Draft approach we'll produce by EOD Friday:
1) Workload carve-out matrix: define 3 service classes (latency-sensitive chat, high-throughput embedding, background rerank) with hard concurrency caps and admission-control policies.
2) Thermal-aware headroom: compute sustained derate factor from telemetry and vendor thermal curves, then apply a 15–25% safety margin depending on rack cooling spec.
3) NIC & egress constraint: recommend per-rack safe QPS and token egress ceilings (we'll produce a simple formula: tokens/sec * avg bytes/token + replication overhead).
4) Autoscale + warm-cache policy: suggest warm pool sizes per class, plus a canary scale-up test to validate CPU/GPU temperature drift.

Action items for Orchid:
- Confirm whether you want a hard SLA for p95 latency on chat (e.g., 300–500ms) or a softer SLO.
- Share any constraints on acceptable overcommit (we assume <= 1.5x logical overcommit during non-peak).

I'm attaching a placeholder matrix (carveout-capacity-matrix-v1.xlsx) and a rack thermal image we used for a similar customer. Rishi, Karthik, and Laura will add sizing numbers and an operational checklist.

Best,

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Evan Turner <evan.turner@orchid-ai.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-12-11T11:18:00Z
Subject: Re: Private GPU pool: thermal behavior and throughput targets

Evan / team —

I ran the numbers against the telemetry and vendor thermal curves. High-level recommendations (summary — we'll include the worksheets and formulas in the Drive doc):

1) Classification and baseline per-GPU throughput assumptions
   - Low-latency chat (class A): median seq 512, p95 request length 1024. For the model family you're planning (quantized 70B), assume sustained single-GPU steady-state throughput of ~220 tokens/sec for interactive decoding when unconstrained, but apply a sustained-thermal derate factor of 0.82 for long windows (>45min) in your ambient.
   - Embedding batches (class B): high token throughput per call but highly parallelizable. Treat these as batch slots; effective tokens/sec per GPU can be 3–4x transiently.
   - Background rerank (class C): low concurrency, heavy memory; capacity is often limited by PCIe and host CPU pre/post-processing rather than raw token throughput.

2) Headroom & pool sizing formula
   - Target peak demand (from telemetry): ~6.5M tokens/min across all classes.
   - Effective tokens/sec per GPU (operational) = nominal_tokens_sec * derate * (1 / tail_slowdown_multiplier). Use tail_slowdown_multiplier = 1.2 for p95 budgeting.
   - Using the numbers above, plan for N = ceil(peak_tokens_sec / (220 * 0.82 / 1.2)). This yields an initial committed pool in the low-to-mid double digits (we include an example sheet showing 36 GPUs for a conservative read).

3) Thermal & cooling controls
   - Add an automated thermal governor: when per-rack average GPU power exceeds threshold for >20 minutes, begin shedding best-effort embedding batches first (class B), then reduce concurrency of class C. Preserve class A at target p95 with QoS token caps.
   - Schedule a 90-minute warmup test in staging to measure real drift and validate the 0.82 derate number; if measured derate is worse than 0.75, increase the committed pool by +20%.

4) Network & NIC headroom
   - Recommend keeping uplink utilization <= 60% sustained. For a 40 Gbps link, cap long-lived egress to 24 Gbps. Convert tokens->bytes conservatively at 8 bytes/token + 12% protocol overhead, then add inter-rack replication buffer.

5) Autoscale and admission control
   - Use two thresholds: fast path (scale-up when queue length > 10% for >30s) and slow path (add one GPU when sustained cpu/gpu busy > 85% for 3min). Prefer vertical warm-spare (reserve 2–4 GPUs per rack) to avoid cross-rack scheduling when latency-sensitive.

6) Operational checklist (short)
   - Canary: warm cache, run 30m steady-load at 80% expected peak, capture temp drift.
   - Alerts: per-GPU thermals, p95 latency per class, per-rack uplink utilization.
   - Runbooks: warm-pool preflight, emergency scale-down that preserves class A.

I'll add the worked spreadsheet to the Drive link and include the formulas we used. Laura, would you own the SLA language and the playbook steps with InfraOps?

- Rishi

Evan —

Thanks for the clear ask and the telemetry. The recommendations from Rishi look right for an initial committed pool. Next steps from Redwood side:

1) We'll finalize the carve-out matrix (deliverable: Carveout + Admission Control runbook) by 2026-12-16.
2) InfraOps schedule: please confirm a 2-hour window in staging next week for the 90-minute warmup test (we need full GPU telemetry and rack thermal sensors enabled).
3) Security/Procurement: once you confirm acceptable overcommit and SLA bounds I'll produce the committed capacity attachment for your purchase order.

Operational caveats to note to Orchid: sustained heavy batch runs will increase the likelihood of thermal plateauing; without additional cooling, you should expect the effective capacity to vary over multi-hour windows. We recommend the +15% contractual headroom and a documented failover policy that prioritizes chat.

Evan — can you confirm the staging window and whether Orchid wants Redwood to operate the warm-pool for the first 30 days? If yes, we'll include a staffed-runbook and runbook handoff.
